chunks: And it is reported from Luqman (peace be upon him) that he said:

To his son: 'O my son! I tasted patience and ate the bark of trees, but I did not find anything more bitter than poverty. So if you are tried by it for a day, do not manifest it to the people, lest they belittle you and not benefit you with anything. Return to the One who tested you with it, for He is more able to provide your relief, and ask Him. [Consider] the one who asked Him and was not given [what he wanted], or relied upon Him but was not rescued.'
ai.seo_question: What is Luqman's advice on how to handle poverty and what to show to people?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Luqman al-Hakim illustrates the profound bitterness of poverty, advising his son to practice *istikhfa'* (concealment) rather than *istifqa'* (open begging) to preserve dignity and avoid being taken for granted by others. This guidance underscores the Shia emphasis on self-reliance and trusting in God’s capacity to provide, linking the physical hardship of poverty with the spiritual discipline of patience (*sabr*). The advice reflects the broader ethical framework where enduring hardship with grace is superior to actively seeking relief from creation.

en.hubeali: And it is reported from Luqman<sup>as</sup>

who<sup>as</sup> said to his<sup>as</sup> son: ‘O my<sup>as</sup> son! I<sup>as</sup> tasted the patience and ate the bark of the tree, but I<sup>as</sup> did not find anything which more bitter than the poverty. So if you are tried by it one day, do not manifest it to the people, for they would be belittling you, and they will not be benefitting you with anything. Place your hope to the One<sup>azwj</sup> Who Tried you with it, for He<sup>azwj</sup> is more Able upon your relief, and ask Him<sup>azwj</sup>. The one who asked Him<sup>azwj</sup> and was not Given it, or relied upon Him<sup>azwj</sup> but was not rescued (How come)?’
en.sarwar: to his son, ‘Son, I have tested patience and have consumed tree barks for food. I have not found anything as bitter as poverty. If you ever face poverty, do not tell people about it; you will seem insignificant in their sight and they will be of no benefit to you. You must turn to the One who has placed it upon you as a trial. He has all the power to grant you relief, but you must ask Him for help. No one asking Him for help is ever turned away empty-handed, and no one who has placed his trust in Him is ever abandoned.’”
